faire-direct-vs-marketplace.html.text:
FAIRE DIRECT VS MARKETPLACE

The 15% is not the whole decision. The first-order fee and Direct are.

Faire publishes a 15% marketplace commission. That number is what most “Faire fees” pages stop at. A brand pricing an opening order also pays a one-time new-customer fee (Faire’s North America help article lists $10; outside North America it is an extra 10% on that first order). A retailer you already know can order through your Faire Direct link at 0% commission. Processing still comes out of every Faire payout.

The Faire seller fee calculator runs those three paths — plus an off-Faire invoice — on one wholesale order. The table below is the default example ($20 wholesale × 10 units, $8 cost, $15 shipping both ways, 60-day payout). Replace the numbers on the calculator with your payout summary.

Path Commission shape What changes on the same invoice
Marketplace first order 15% + new-customer fee The expensive introduction. Price wholesale so this path still clears your floor.
Marketplace reorder 15% only Same retailer, no new-customer fee. This is the repeating Faire path.
Faire Direct 0% commission You brought the retailer. Processing remains. Use this to price existing accounts you move onto Faire.
Own invoice None unless you charge cards A comparison only — you keep payment risk and collections. Not a recommendation to leave Faire.

Payment processing is the other lever. Faire’s public North America article lists 3.5% + $0.30 next day, 2.4% + $0.30 at 30 days, and 1.9% + $0.30 at 60 days. The calculator’s payout-speed table holds the order still and changes only that line. If you expect the same retailer to come back, set expected reorders on the calculator: the first-order fee is then shown amortized across that relationship, next to the same number of Direct or off-Faire invoices.

Independent retailers have a different job: landed cost versus shelf price after opening-order discounts and unsold units. That is the retailer margin calculator. Brands deciding whether a seasonal 0% window still pays after a deeper retailer discount use Open House vs everyday first order.

Common questions

What is Faire Direct?

Faire Direct is Faire's published 0% commission path for retailers you bring to the marketplace with your personalized link. Payment processing still applies. Marketplace orders from retailers who found you on Faire pay the standard commission, and a first marketplace order also includes the one-time new-customer fee.

Is Faire Direct cheaper than the marketplace?

On the same invoice, Direct has no commission, so net payout is higher before you count the work of finding the retailer yourself. Use the calculator with your own cost and payout speed. This page does not tell you which path to use.

Does the Faire first-order fee matter if a retailer reorders?

The new-customer fee is one-time. The brand calculator amortizes it across the opening order plus the reorders you expect from that retailer, and compares that lifetime to sending every order through Faire Direct or your own invoice. Enter the reorder count you actually see — this page does not forecast repeat purchase.

What this checks

Generic “Faire fee calculator” pages stop at 15%. The decision a brand actually faces is whether a first marketplace order still works after the new-customer fee, how that fee looks after the reorders you expect from the same retailer, whether a Faire Direct link is worth sending to an existing account, whether Open House still leaves more after the deeper discount retailers expect, whether Promoted Listings still cover last-click organic first orders, whether a keep-it credit still beats taking the return after a completed first order, whether a Pay Now discount still covers Faire remittance wait, and whether next-day payout still beats waiting after the carrying cost you type. A boutique buying the same order has a different question: landed cost versus shelf price.

It does not recommend a wholesale price, a payout speed, or a channel, and it is not tax or financial advice. The gaps are an arithmetic comparison of the rates you entered.

Common questions

How much does Faire charge sellers?

Faire publishes a 15% marketplace commission. North American brands also pay a one-time $10 new-customer fee on a retailer's first marketplace order. Brands outside North America pay an extra 10% on that first order instead of $10. Faire Direct orders from retailers you bring yourself are 0% commission. Payment processing is separate and depends on payout speed. Enter the rates from your payout summary — this page does not publish Faire's live schedule.

What is the difference between a Faire first order and a reorder?

A first marketplace order from a new retailer includes the one-time new-customer fee on top of the standard commission. Later orders from that same retailer do not. Faire Direct is a third path: 0% commission when the retailer used your Direct link. This calculator shows all three on the same order so you can see whether the first-order fee changes the wholesale price you need.

Does Faire charge commission on brand-funded discounts?

Faire's published payout formula takes commission on the order subtotal after brand-funded promotions. This calculator subtracts your discount percentage before applying commission and processing. Verify against the payout summary on the order.

How does the Faire new-customer fee look after a retailer reorders?

The new-customer fee is charged once. Enter how many reorders you expect from that retailer to see lifetime marketplace profit next to the same number of Faire Direct or off-Faire invoices, and the first-order fee divided across those orders. This is arithmetic from your count, not a forecast that they will reorder.

Is Faire next-day payout worth the extra processing fee?

On the calculator defaults — a $200 North America first marketplace order and a 24% annual carrying-cost assumption — next-day payout leaves $72.59 after modeled float. Waiting 60 days leaves $69.28. The $3.20 processing spread does not cover 24% money sitting 60 days. At 6%, waiting still finishes ahead. Enter your own rate. This is not a recommendation to take next-day payout.

Should I take this Faire return?

On a completed $20 × 10 first order that booked $75.90, a 20% keep-it credit leaves $41.90. Denying at 50% they'll-drop-it leaves $37.95. Taking all 10 units back with an $18 label and 80% restockable leaves −$49.00. Returning 2 of 10 with an $8 label flips taking the return to $46.52. This is not a recommendation to take, credit, or fight the return.

Does Faire Open House still leave more after a deeper opening discount?

Faire Open House typically waives marketplace commission for a short window. Retailers often expect a deeper brand-funded discount during that window. On the calculator defaults a $20 × 10 first order keeps $75.90 everyday after 15% + $10, $66.66 during Open House at 20% off (−$9.24), and $105.90 if you keep your everyday discount. The waived commission funds about 15.3% off before leftover matches everyday. Two extra new retailers flip the 20% path to $199.98 vs $75.90. This is not Faire Direct — you still did not bring the retailer — and it is not a forecast that the window will produce those extra accounts.

Should I offer Faire Pay Now?

On the calculator defaults — a $20 × 10 first marketplace order, a 2% Pay Now discount, 40% take-rate, and 24% money — skipping Pay Now keeps $69.16 after 60-day remittance. Offering it keeps $67.88 (−$1.28). Everyone taking it keeps $65.96. The 2% matches if Pay Now remittance falls to about 31.0 days or extra first orders rise to about 0.02. One extra first order flips the offer to $133.85. A 1-day remittance flips everyone-takes to $72.47. This is not next-day payout and not generic 2/10 Net 30.

Are Faire Promoted Listings worth it?

On the calculator defaults — four organic $20 × 10 first orders, one extra first order, a 15% promoted rate, and 40% last-click attribution on organic — skipping the campaign keeps $303.60 and running it keeps $301.50 (−$2.10). Ads match if the rate falls to about 14.6%, extra first orders rise to about 1.0, or last-click attribution on organic falls to about 38.3%. Two extra first orders flip the campaign to $347.40. This page does the arithmetic from the rates you enter; it does not recommend turning a campaign on.

Should I list during Faire Open House?

Brands search this when Faire waives marketplace commission for a short window and retailers expect a deeper opening discount. Listing everyday at 15% + the new-customer fee is the baseline. Open House is not Faire Direct — you still did not bring the retailer — and it is not a reorder. The main calculator’s first-order table cannot show whether the waived commission pays for the extra markdown.

On the default $20 × 10 first order, everyday keeps $75.90 after 15% + $10. Open House at 0% commission and a 20% retailer discount keeps $66.66 (−$9.24). The waived commission still funds about 15.3% off before leftover matches everyday. Keep your everyday discount during the window and leftover is $105.90 (+$30.00) — the leak is the deeper discount, not the event. Two extra new retailers flip the 20% path to $199.98 vs $75.90 (+$124.08). Two Open House first orders (1 extra) match one everyday order.

Window Discount First-order leftover vs everyday Window leftover

First-order leftover is one new retailer. Window leftover multiplies the Open House rows by 1 + extra new retailers — a count you type, not a forecast that the event will produce them. Complementary to Faire Direct (you brought the account), to a keep-it credit vs taking the return after the order lands, and to the brand calculator lifetime table (reorders after the opening fee). Paste the Open House commission and discount from the event terms on your account. This page does not publish Faire’s live Open House schedule.

The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend listing during Open House, waiting, or deepening a discount.

Common questions

Should I list during Faire Open House?

On the calculator defaults — a $20 wholesale unit × 10, $8 cost, $15 shipping both ways, 15% commission, $10 new-customer fee, 60-day processing — an everyday first order keeps $75.90. Open House at 0% commission and a 20% retailer discount keeps $66.66 (−$9.24). The waived commission still funds about 15.3% off before leftover matches everyday. Open House at your everyday 0% discount keeps $105.90 (+$30.00). Two extra new retailers flip the 20% path to $199.98 vs $75.90 (+$124.08). Two Open House first orders (1 extra) match one everyday order.

Is Faire Open House the same as Faire Direct?

No. Faire Direct is 0% commission when you bring the retailer with your link. Open House is a seasonal window when Faire typically waives marketplace commission on retailers who still found you on Faire. The new-customer fee can still apply. This page holds Direct and off-Faire invoices off the table so the comparison stays an everyday-versus-event first-order question.

When does a deeper Open House discount still beat listing everyday?

When you already fund an everyday opening discount, or when the window actually produces extra new first orders. On these defaults a 20% event discount loses $9.24 per order against an everyday 0% list, but two extra new retailers flip the pile by $124.08. If you already list at 15% off everyday, the 20% Open House path wins per order. Paste the Open House commission and discount from the event terms on your account — this page does not publish Faire's live Open House schedule.

Should I offer Faire Pay Now?

Brands search this when Faire offers a brand-funded extra percent so retailers pay immediately instead of Net terms. Next-day payout is a different fee: you pay Faire more processing so your remittance arrives sooner. Generic 2/10 Net 30 is a third path — it has no marketplace commission on the discounted subtotal. This page is not next-day payout and not Faire Direct.

On the default $20 × 10 first order, skipping a 2% Pay Now discount keeps $69.16 after 60-day remittance and 24% money. Offering it at a 40% take-rate keeps $67.88 (−$1.28). Everyone taking it keeps $65.96. The 2% matches if Pay Now remittance falls to about 31.0 days or extra first orders rise to about 0.02. One extra first order flips the offer to $133.85 (+$64.69). A 1-day remittance flips everyone-takes to $72.47 (+$3.31). Mixed take at that 1-day remittance keeps $70.48.

Pay Now path Pay Now % Remit days Pay Now leftover vs Net terms

Leftover is first-order profit minus modeled carrying cost on the Faire payout for the remittance days you type. Pay Now is an extra percent stacked on your opening discount so the listing promo cannot hide the early-pay cost. Extra first orders are a count you type, not a forecast that the discount will produce them. Complementary to next-day payout (processing you pay Faire) and to generic 2/10 Net 30 (no marketplace commission). Paste remittance days from your payout summary. This page does not publish Faire’s live Pay Now schedule.

The calculator is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend turning Pay Now on, raising the discount, or skipping it.

Should I offer Faire Pay Now?

Offering it keeps $67.88 (−$1.28). Everyone taking it keeps $65.96. The 2% matches if Pay Now remittance falls to about 31.0 days or extra first orders rise to about 0.02. This page does the arithmetic from the rates you enter; it does not recommend turning Pay Now on.

Is Faire Pay Now the same as next-day payout?

No. Next-day payout is a processing percent you pay Faire so your remittance arrives sooner. Pay Now is a brand-funded extra percent so the retailer pays Faire immediately. Faire can still remit to you on your payout schedule. Generic 2/10 Net 30 is a third path: it has no marketplace commission on the discounted subtotal. This page holds those off the table so the comparison stays skip-versus-Pay Now.

When remittance actually lands sooner or extra first orders cover the 2%. On these defaults the same 60-day remittance loses $1.28 against skip. should-i-pay-for-faire-next-day-payout.h.text:
← Faire seller fee calculator

Should I pay for Faire next-day payout?

Brands search this after Faire offers three payout speeds on the same invoice. Next-day processing is 3.5% + $0.30. Waiting 60 days is 1.9% + $0.30. The slower line looks cheaper until the cash you already spent on goods sits unpaid.

The processing spread is small. The wait is not. On the calculator defaults — a $200 North America first marketplace order ($20 wholesale × 10, $8 cost, $15 shipping both ways, the $10 new-customer fee) — next-day processing is $7.30 and 60-day processing is $4.10. That is a $3.20 spread. Next-day cash is $167.70. Waiting 60 days pays $170.90.

24% money makes next-day payout the cheaper path. A card, merchant-cash-advance, or inventory line at 24% models $6.62 of carrying cost on that $167.70 over 60 days. Next-day leaves $72.59 after $0.11 of one-day float. Waiting 60 days leaves $69.28 — $3.31 behind. Next-day and 60-day match at about 11.8%.

Cheap capital still covers the wait. At 6%, the same 60-day wait models $1.65 of float and leaves $74.25. Next-day leaves $72.67. The $3.20 processing savings still covers 6% money.

Path Wait Profit Carrying at 24% After float
Next-day payout1 day$72.70$0.11$72.59
30-day payout30 days$74.90$3.31$71.59
60-day payout60 days$75.90$6.62$69.28

What this number is not

Carrying cost is your assumption, not a Faire fee and not interest you can invoice a retailer. Faire's published processing is a payout-speed fee. Confirm the rate on the payout summary. The calculator does not pick a speed for you.

Open the Faire seller fee calculator, keep your wholesale price and cost, and type the annual rate you actually pay. A Faire Direct vs marketplace comparison is a different question: commission path, not when the cash lands.

Common questions

Is Faire next-day payout worth the extra processing fee?

On the calculator defaults — a $200 North America first marketplace order ($20 wholesale, 10 units, $8 cost, $15 shipping both ways) and a 24% annual carrying-cost assumption — next-day payout leaves $72.59 after $0.11 of modeled float. Waiting 60 days leaves $69.28 after $6.62 of float. The $3.20 processing spread does not cover 24% money sitting 60 days on the $167.70 you could have had next day.

When does waiting 60 days for Faire payout still pay?

When your money is cheap. At a 6% annual carrying-cost assumption the same order leaves $74.25 after waiting and $72.67 next day. Next-day and 60-day match at about 11.8%. Enter the rate you actually pay on a card, inventory line, or opportunity cost. This page does not tell you which payout speed to pick.

Does Faire charge interest for 60-day payout?

No. Faire's published processing is a payout-speed fee (3.5% + $0.30 next day, 2.4% + $0.30 at 30 days, 1.9% + $0.30 at 60 days), not interest. The carrying-cost line is your own assumption applied to the cash you forgo by waiting. Confirm every fee against the payout summary on the order.

This is not Open House and not Faire Direct. Those pages price listing and the channel. This page starts after a completed first marketplace order, when the retailer wants goods back.

On the calculator defaults — $20 × 10, $8 cost, $15 shipping both ways, 15% + $10, 60-day processing, already booked $75.90 — a 20% keep-it credit leaves $41.90 after reversing $6.00 of commission. Denying at 50% they'll-drop-it leaves $37.95. Taking all 10 units back with an $18.00 label and 80% restockable leaves −$49.00. Denying matches the credit at about 55.2% they'll-drop-it.

Returning 2 of 10 with an $8 label flips taking the return to $46.52. Denying at 70% flips ahead to $53.13.

Choice Leftover vs keep-it

The first-order fee and outbound label are already sunk on the completed order. Taking the return claws back that slice of payout and recovers only restockable COGS. The keep-it credit reverses commission on the credited merchandise, not the $10 new-customer fee. Complementary to Should I list during Faire Open House? and Faire Direct vs marketplace. Open the Faire seller fee calculator to change the wholesale price.

Common questions

Should I take this Faire return?

On the calculator defaults — a completed $20 × 10 first marketplace order that booked $75.90, a 20% keep-it credit, 50% they'll-drop-it if you deny, an $18 return label, and 80% restockable — the keep-it credit leaves $41.90. Denying leaves $37.95. Taking the full return leaves −$49.00 because outbound shipping and the $10 new-customer fee are already sunk. This is not a recommendation to take, credit, or fight the return.

When does taking a Faire return still beat a keep-it credit?

When only some units come back. Returning 2 of 10 with an $8 label leaves $46.52 and flips ahead of the $41.90 keep-it credit. A full return at these costs does not. Denying at 70% they'll-drop-it leaves $53.13 and flips ahead of the credit.

Is a Faire return the same as Open House or Faire Direct?

No. Open House is whether to list during a 0% commission window. Faire Direct is 0% commission when you bring the retailer. This page starts after a completed first order, when the retailer wants goods back.

vs-ankorstore.html.text:
THIS CALCULATOR VS ANKORSTORE

Two different marketplaces. This tool prices Faire orders specifically.

Ankorstore is a separate B2B wholesale marketplace, not a competitor to this calculator — it is a competitor to Faire itself. Founded in France in November 2019, Ankorstore grew to unicorn status on a large funding round led by Index Ventures, and connects independent brands with retailers mainly across Europe, with its own commission structure that it has continued to change (it simplified its pricing and moved to 0% commission on reorders in January 2026, according to its own published updates). Ankorstore's current full rate card is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact figures, so none of its numbers are entered here or invented on this page — only its well-documented identity and category are stated.

This calculator does not price an Ankorstore order at all. It is built specifically from Faire's own published North America fee schedule — the 15% marketplace commission, the one-time $10 new-customer fee on a retailer's first order, Faire Direct's 0% commission for retailers you bring yourself, and Faire's payout-speed processing rates — and turns one wholesale invoice into net payout, margin, and ROI across those Faire-specific paths. A brand selling through both marketplaces owes each one its own separate fees on its own orders; this tool does not combine, convert, or compare the two marketplaces' rates against each other.

Question Where to answer it
What does my Faire order net after commission, the new-customer fee, and payout speed? This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
What does my Ankorstore order net after its commission and payout terms? Ankorstore's own current rate card and calculator — this tool does not model Ankorstore's fees.
Should I sell on Faire, Ankorstore, both, or neither? That is a market-fit and reach decision this page does not make. Compare each marketplace's own published terms and your own retailer mix.
Is Faire Direct cheaper than a Faire marketplace order? See Faire Direct vs Marketplace on this same calculator.

Common questions

Is Ankorstore the same thing as Faire?

No. Both are B2B wholesale marketplaces connecting independent brands with retailers, but they are separate companies with separate commission structures, separate retailer bases, and separate payout mechanics. Ankorstore was founded in France in 2019 and reached unicorn status backed by Index Ventures, focused heavily on European brands and retailers; Faire is a separate marketplace with its own published North American fee schedule. A brand selling on both would owe each marketplace its own fees on its own orders — this calculator does not combine or convert between the two.

Does this calculator work out my Ankorstore fees too?

No. This calculator's commission, new-customer fee, and payout-speed math is built specifically from Faire's own published North America fee schedule. Ankorstore publishes its own separate rates, which change independently of Faire's and are not reachable from this session to confirm today's figures, so none of Ankorstore's numbers are entered here or invented on this page. If you sell on Ankorstore, use its own current rate card and calculator.

vs-building-your-own-spreadsheet.html.text:
THIS CALCULATOR VS A SPREADSHEET

One fee formula is easy. Amortizing it across a relationship is the part that gets skipped.

A spreadsheet handles a single Faire order correctly once you build the formula: order subtotal times commission rate, plus a processing percentage and a fixed fee, subtracted from what you're owed. That much is one row of arithmetic and a careful seller gets it exactly right. Where a from-scratch spreadsheet usually stops is the step past a single order — the one-time new-customer fee applies only to a retailer's first marketplace order, not every order from them, and most sellers either forget to drop it after order one or never build the formula to track it at all.

This calculator takes the same inputs — wholesale price, quantity, cost of goods, your fee rates — and adds the two comparisons a single-order formula doesn't give you: lifetime profit on a retailer across an opening order plus however many reorders you expect, priced against sending every one of those orders through Faire Direct or your own invoice instead; and the wholesale price that hits a target margin, solved backward from your costs and fee rates rather than guessed at and checked by hand.

Question Where to answer it
What does one Faire order net after commission and processing? Either — a spreadsheet built correctly gets this exactly right, too.
What does a retailer relationship net across an opening order plus reorders, once the new-customer fee only hits the first one? This calculator's lifetime comparison — a spreadsheet needs a second, deliberately built formula to track when the fee stops applying.
What wholesale price hits a specific margin, given my costs and fee rates? This calculator solves it directly. By hand, it's algebra you have to set up and re-check every time a rate or cost changes.
How many reorders would it take to make a loss-making first order worth it? This calculator's break-even count — most from-scratch spreadsheets never get a formula built for this at all.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere? No, either way — a local spreadsheet and this calculator both keep your numbers on your own device.

Common questions

Can't I just work out Faire fees in a spreadsheet?

For one order, yes — commission is order subtotal times rate, processing is another percentage plus a fixed fee, and payout is what's left. Any spreadsheet gets that arithmetic exactly right. Where a spreadsheet built from scratch usually falls short is a retailer relationship across more than one order: the new-customer fee only applies to the first marketplace order, and dividing it evenly across every order, or forgetting it lapses after the first, both understate or overstate what a reorder is actually worth.

What does this calculator do that a spreadsheet formula usually misses?

Two things specifically. First, lifetime profit on a retailer: this calculator prices the opening order with the one-time new-customer fee, prices every reorder without it, and sums them against sending the same order count through Faire Direct or your own invoice instead — a comparison a spreadsheet has to be deliberately built to run, not something a single fee formula gives you. Second, it solves backward: given a target margin, cash costs, and your fee rates, it works out the wholesale price that hits that margin, which is algebra most sellers don't set up correctly on the first try and have to re-derive by hand every time a rate or cost changes.

Is the wholesale price for a target margin something I could solve myself?

With the right algebra, yes — it means isolating wholesale price on one side of the payout equation after the flat first-order fee, the percentage fees, and your cash cost are all accounted for, then dividing back out any brand-funded discount. Setting that up correctly, and getting it right again after a commission or discount rate changes, is exactly the one-time-easy, easy-to-get-subtly-wrong-later math this calculator removes. Getting a sign wrong on the discount term is not obvious in the output the way a typo in a price is.

Does a spreadsheet see how many reorders it takes to break even?

Only if you build a formula for it. When a first order posts a loss after the new-customer fee, this calculator works out how many reorders at the standard rate would bring cumulative profit positive — a small division, but one more step past the fee formula itself, and one most from-scratch spreadsheets skip because nobody thought to ask the question until the first order was already unprofitable.

Is this page affiliated with any spreadsheet software?

There is nothing to be affiliated with. This page compares against building your own spreadsheet formulas — a generic method every seller already has access to, not any specific company or product — so it names no spreadsheet application or vendor at all.
